msIdentifier.msName: Codex Argenteus (so named by Bonaventura Vulcanius in 1597)
Fragmentum Spirense / Folium Spirense / Haffner folium (after its discoverer)

summary.p: The codex is a Gospel book, with the Gospels arranged in the so-called "Western" order (Matthew, John, Luke, and Mark). The leaf preserved at Speyer transmits Mark 16:12-20.

msItem.title: Gospel of Matthew
msItem.note: 98 leaves originally; 22 survive (approximately 75% lost). Surviving passages: Mt 5:15-6:32; 7:12-10:1; 10:23-11:25; 26:70-27:19; 27:42-66 (corresponding to approximately 25% of Matthew).

msItem.title: Gospel of John
msItem.note: 74 leaves originally; 45 survive (approximately 40% lost). Surviving passages: Jn 5:45-7:52; 8:12-11:47; 12:1-49; 13:11-19:13 (corresponding to approximately 60% of John).

msItem.title: Gospel of Luke
msItem.note: 106 leaves originally; 70 survive (approximately 35% lost). Surviving passages: Lk 1:1-10:30; 14:9-16:24; 17:3-20:46 (corresponding to approximately 65% of Luke).

msItem.title: Gospel of Mark
msItem.note: 58 leaves originally; 51 survive in Uppsala (approximately 8% lost). Surviving passages: Mk 1:1-6:30; 6:53-12:38; 13:16-29; 14:4-16; 14:41-16:11 (corresponding to approximately 92% of Mark).

msItem.title: Gospel of Mark (conclusion)
msItem.note: One leaf preserved at Speyer, containing Mark 16:12-20. The presence of wormholes suggests it originally followed a wooden board, constituting the final leaf of the codex.

support.p: The parchment is extremely thin and prepared with great care. Its colour is purple: for the dyeing—varying from leaf to leaf and between hair side and flesh side—both orchil and indigo were most likely used (Aceto et al. 2019, 137-138). Visual inspection further suggests a combined use of orchil in the margins and folium in the written area.
In 1998 the parchment was subjected to radiocarbon (C-14) analysis in order to establish its date; the result indicates a date not later than 550 (Possnert-Munkhammar 2002).

extent.p: The manuscript originally consisted of 336 leaves (Friesen-Grape 1928, 35), of which 187 are preserved at Uppsala and one leaf at Speyer. The Gospel of Matthew comprised 98 leaves (22 survive), the Gospel of John 74 leaves (45 survive), the Gospel of Luke 106 leaves (70 survive), and the Gospel of Mark 58 leaves (51 survive).

foliation.p: The leaves were numbered in pencil in the upper outer margin after they had been disbound and rebound in the order of the Vulgate (Gospel of Matthew, Gospel of Mark, Gospel of Luke, and Gospel of John), as already attested in the editio princeps (1665). This new foliation dates to the nineteenth century.

collation.p: The gatherings are mostly quaternions, except for the final gathering of each Gospel. Of the original gatherings, 37 were therefore quaternions and four quinions. The quire structure follows Gregory's rule (flesh facing flesh and hair facing hair).
The quire number indicating the order of the gatherings, preserved only in some cases, is placed in the lower right corner of the last leaf of the gathering, enclosed within a frame of signs.

condition.p: The codex is now disbound; each leaf is placed in a cardboard folder and kept in a safe. The manuscript is generally in good condition, except for some leaves that have suffered from humidity. The ink of the final leaf (from Speyer) is very faded. No traces of the original binding survive.

layout.p: The text is arranged in a single column, in scriptio continua, except for the "Genealogy of Jesus" (Lk 3:23-38), which is laid out in two columns.
The ruling was executed dry-point, apparently one bifolium at a time, on the flesh side. The written area is delimited by a single marginal ruling line and is divided horizontally into two sections.
The upper section, intended for the text, is divided into 20 lines on which the letters rest, bounded above by an additional ruling line.

The lower section, which contains the canon tables, begins one centimetre below the last line of the upper system and is divided into 11 evenly spaced lines. Pricking marks for the ruling are not visible. The overall proportions of the text area and the canon tables follow the principle of the "golden section" (ca. 210 × 130 mm).

handDesc.handNote: The first scribe (hand I) wrote the Gospels of Matthew and John. The manuscript is written in the vertical Gothic script (with <s> of Latin form), set within an actually ruled bilinear system. The hand is very regular.
The second scribe (hand II) wrote the Gospels of Luke and Mark. The hand is very regular, but slightly more slender than hand I.

Fifteen marginal glosses are present, also in silver ink and in the vertical script type, perhaps added in the same scriptorium in which the manuscript was produced. It is difficult to determine with certainty whether they are by hands different from those of the text.

scriptDesc.p: The manuscript is written in the vertical Gothic script (with <s> of Latin form), set within an actually ruled bilinear system. The letter marking the beginning of a new textual unit is written in a larger module, both when it coincides with the beginning of a new line (in which case it is partially or entirely shifted outside the outer vertical ruling) and, more rarely and with less enlargement, within the line. Letters of smaller module and, very rarely, ligatures (for mu, ht, rþ, þr) occur at line end.

decoDesc.decoNote: Architectural frames of simplified form, drawn in silver ink and without painted completion, appear at the foot of the page; they contain the Eusebian canon tables.

Only the colophon of the Gospel of Mark has been preserved: aiwaggeljo · þ(ai)rh · m(a)r(ku) · | ustauh · wulþus · þus | weiha · g(u)þ · amen · "The Gospel according to Mark is finished. Glory to you, O holy God. Amen." The letters are more widely spaced and slightly larger than those of the text.

additions.p: Titles: Only the titles of the Gospels of Luke and Mark are preserved: aiwaggeljo · þairh · lukan · anastodeiþ "The Gospel according to Luke begins" (f. 118r) and aiwaggeljo · þairh marku · anastodeiþ "The Gospel according to Mark begins" (f. 57r). They are written in silver ink, in a slightly smaller module and in a more compressed form than the text script.

Running titles: placed every two leaves in the upper central margin on the flesh side and rest on a ruling line. On the verso appears þairh, and on the facing recto the abbreviated form of the evangelist's name.

Eusebian sections and canon tables: The text of each Gospel is divided into sections numbered consecutively (355 in Matthew, 233 in Mark, 342 in Luke, and 232 in John). The section numbers are indicated in the left margin of the leaf, enclosed within a frame of signs. Canon tables are placed in the lower part of each page.
Paragraph mark: written in gold ink, consists of a thin horizontal stroke thickened at both ends, with at its centre a sign resembling a dot or a diplé, placed in the left margin.
Quotation mark: Quotations from the Old Testament are indicated by the diplé (>), in silver ink, placed in the left margin outside the written area and extending along the entire quotation.

Punctuation: The medial point marks minor pauses (commata), and the colon marks major pauses (cola). Occasionally, in the Gospel of Luke, the colon is written in two different inks when followed by an Eusebian section.
Orthography: Orthographic variations are attested that are also common in other Gothic manuscripts; the most frequent are <e> for <ei>, occasionally for <i>; <au> for <u>; <d> for <þ>.

Abbreviations and contractions: Both nasals are abbreviated at line end. Nomina sacra for "God", "Lord", "Jesus", and "Christ" are present in contracted form. The names of the evangelists in the running titles are abbreviated. In the canon tables, the names of Matthew and Mark are represented by monograms.
Numerals: expressed according to Greek usage by letters, placed between points and surmounted by a horizontal stroke when they occur in the text.

Corrections: Occasional corrections consist of erasures and rewritings of individual letters, or of additions in the interlinear space and, in one case, in the margin (f. 61v). They are plausibly contemporary and by the same scribe as the text since they too are written in silver ink. Not all errors were corrected.
Glosses: Fifteen marginal glosses in silver ink, perhaps added in the same scriptorium. Framed above by a reference mark and below, occasionally, by a descending flourish.

seal.p: Two different ink colours are used in the manuscript. Silver ink: main body of text, Gospel titles, running titles, quotation marks, numbers of Eusebian sections, canon tables. Gold ink: first three lines of each Gospel (Luke and Mark preserved), beginning of each Eusebian section up to end of line, paragraph mark, abbreviations of evangelists' names in canon tables, and the first line of the Lord's Prayer (Mt 6:9). In some places both ink and parchment are damaged, possibly indicating the presence of an acidic or corrosive substance in the ink.

origin.origDate: First quarter of the sixth century
origin.origPlace: It is likely that the manuscript was copied in Ravenna, the capital of the Ostrogothic kingdom and an important cultural centre.
origin.p: The Codex Argenteus is the principal witness to the Gothic translation of the Gospels traditionally attributed to the Visigothic bishop Wulfila. The refinement of the codex suggests a patron of high status, commonly identified with Theoderic the Great (†526) and the palatine church.

It has often been hypothesised that the Argenteus originally constituted the Gothic part of a bilingual Gothic-Latin Gospel book in separate volumes, whose Latin counterpart would be the Codex Brixianus (Brescia, Biblioteca Queriniana, s.n.). The two manuscripts indeed display non-random codicological and decorative affinities, including the use of purple parchment, silver ink, and architectural arcades at the foot of the page. Certain codicological differences, however, suggest that their production did not take place in parallel (Falluomini 2024).

provenance.p: The history of the Codex Argenteus is known only from the mid-sixteenth century onwards, when its presence at the German monastery of Werden, near Essen, is attested by Georg Cassander and Cornelius Wouters. No information survives as to when or by what route the manuscript arrived there.

At the behest of Emperor Rudolf II, the codex passed—by means that remain obscure—from Werden to Prague and subsequently into Swedish hands as war booty (1648), before being included among the book treasures of Queen Christina of Sweden.

Donated to the queen's librarian, Isaac Vossius, it eventually reached the Netherlands, where it was published for the first time by Vossius' uncle, Franciscus Junius (Quattuor […] evangeliorum versiones perantiquae duae, Gotica scilicet et Anglosaxonica, […], Dordrecht, 1665).

acquisition.p: In 1662 the Swedish count Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie purchased the manuscript and brought it back to Sweden; in 1669 he donated it to Uppsala University, where it is still preserved today.

provenance.p: The final leaf of the Codex Argenteus, containing the conclusion of the Gospel of Mark, came to light in October 1970 at Speyer during restoration work on the Chapel of St Afra. It was preserved inside a casket that also contained relics attributed to Bishop Erasmus of Antioch (Haffner 1971). The wormholes in f. 187 and in the Speyer fragment correspond perfectly. The humanist Philipp Melanchthon handled the leaf in 1518-1519.

surrogates.p: The photographic reproduction, published in 1927, was prepared by Otto von Friesen and Anders Grape. A colour digitisation, curated by Lars Munkhammar, Magnús Snædal, and David Landau, is now available on the website https://www.ub.uu.se/about-the-library/exhibitions/codex-argenteus/.
